subject: Sizing review: private GPU pool for multi-tenant VPC - queueing & headroom
messages:
From: Alex Romero <alex.romero@zephyrsystems.com>
To: tessa.morgan@redwoodinference.com
Cc: cloudops@zephyrsystems.com
Date: Thu, 9 Nov 2028 08:12:00 -0700
Subject: Sizing help: private GPU pool for multi-tenant VPC (throughput and queueing)

Hi Tessa,

Thanks for taking this. We're in the middle of defining sizing for a private VPC deployment of Redwood locally in our AWS account (running in our Dedicated tenancy). A few constraints and goals:

- Multi-tenant pool serving 3 product teams (chat + summarization workloads).
- Expected burst profile: baseline 400 r/s, spike up to 1,800 r/s sustained for ~10-30 minutes during peak events.
- Typical response size: 150-300 tokens; 95th percentile response tokens ~420 tokens.
- Latency SLO target: 95th < 300 ms end-to-end for chat-style completions.
- Networking: traffic enters via NLB in our VPC; egress limits and cross-AZ latency are concerns.

We attached a small trace sample and a rough request timeline. Can you recommend a sizing model (number/type of GPUs), suggested concurrency per GPU, batching/windowing guidance, and how much headroom we should provision before enabling autoscaling? Also interested in recommendations for graceful degradation (fallbacks, quantized variants) and cache-warm strategies to minimize cold-start penalties.

Appreciate a pragmatic plan we can present to infra and procurement.

Alex
Alex Romero
Head of Cloud Engineering, Zephyr Systems

Attachments: zephyr-sample-traces-20281109.txt
From: Tessa Morgan <tessa.morgan@redwoodinference.com>

Cc: marcus.lin@redwoodinference.com, soojin.lee@redwoodinference.com, cloudops@zephyrsystems.com

Subject: Re: Sizing help: private GPU pool for multi-tenant VPC (throughput and queueing)

Alex —

Thanks for the clear brief and the traces. I ran a quick pass with Marcus and Soojin; outline below is a pragmatic, production-friendly starting point you can take to infra/procurement. I attached a simple csv with the proposed node counts and a condensed rationale.

Executive summary (short):
- Recommended starting fleet: 8 H100s (1P) with 30% reserved headroom (i.e., provision for steady-state + 30%). That maps to a warm throughput target of ~120k tokens/sec across the pool assuming per-GPU baseline throughput of ~12k tokens/sec for your 420-token 95th workload if we use batching.
- Autoscale policy: scale on 1-minute aggregated queue length and 95th latency; cooldown 6-8 minutes to avoid flapping. Burst buffer: 2 extra warm GPUs in a cold-warm pool ready to accept traffic for short spikes.
- Fault tolerance: spread across at least 2 AZs, route-by-region with NLB health checks and a connection drain window matching Redwood's batching window (200-400ms).
- Degradation strategy: canonical fallback chain — 1) reduce max tokens (trim long completions) 2) switch to quantized 4-bit variant of same model 3) fallback to smaller verified model with client-side notification header.
- Cache warmup: keep hot KV cache for conversation contexts for 10-15 minutes after last activity; proactively pre-warm KV for expected heavy accounts using synthetic cold runs at T-5 minutes if scheduled.

Sizing rationale (more detail):
- Per-GPU throughput: for your workload shape and sequence length distribution, an H100 (optimized) averages ~10–14k tokens/sec when batching to an effective batch size of 32–48 under our runtime (latency budget permitting). For conservative planning we use 12k tokens/sec.
- Effective request concurrency: with 420 tokens per 95th request and 12k tokens/sec, one GPU can serve ~28 95th-percentile responses/sec (12,000 / 420 ≈ 28.6). For your steady 400 r/s you'd need ~14 GPUs raw, but batching and request token variability reduce real needs; hence the blended 8 GPU starting point with autoscale to handle spikes.
- Headroom: recommend 30% steady headroom plus a quick burst buffer (2 GPUs) for 10–30 minute spikes. This combination limits over-provisioning while keeping SLOs during typical bursts.

Operational suggestions:
- Instrument token-level latency and queue depth per model route; alert on queue depth > 50 per GPU and 95th latency > 250ms.
- Use prefix caching for repeated prompts across product teams (saves ~10–25% tokens depending on overlap).
- Network recommendations: pin inference instances in same AZ as NLB targets; avoid cross-AZ egress for hot traffic. Monitor inter-AZ RTT and re-balance if > 1ms median.

Attachments: gpu-sizing-proposal-20281109.csv
Related links: https://redwood.internal/runbooks/private-gpu-sizing

If useful, Marcus can follow up with the queueing math and a short sim showing expected latency distributions under the proposed policy. Happy to jump on a 30-min call with infra and procurement to finalize the procurement ask.

—Tessa
Tessa Morgan
Head of Partnerships, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Sizing help: private GPU pool for multi-tenant VPC (throughput and queueing)

Alex/Tessa —

Quick queueing model and numeric checks as requested. I'm including a CSV sim (queueing-model-sim-20281109.csv) with a few scenarios; summary below.

Assumptions:
- Service discipline: batching-friendly M/M/c approximation with limited batching window W (we model batching as increasing effective service rate but adding a fixed batching latency <= W).
- Mean tokens per request µ_t = 220; 95th tokens T95 = 420 (use T95 for SLO planning).
- Single H100 service rate r = 12,000 tokens/sec (conservative).

Calculations (95th SLO planning):
- Effective 95th req/sec per GPU = r / T95 = 12,000 / 420 ≈ 28.57 req/s.
- To meet steady 400 r/s with no batching gains you'd need ~15 GPUs (400 / 28.57 ≈ 14.0); however batching at 32–48 windows can raise effective r by ~20–40% for mixed-length workloads.
- With conservative 25% batching gain => per-GPU becomes ~35.7 req/s; GPUs needed for steady 400 r/s => 11.2 => round up to 12.
- Add 30% headroom => 12 * 1.3 ≈ 15.6 => round up to 16 GPU minimum provision for steady+headroom. Add 2 warm burst nodes => 18 total.

Latency breakdown (pessimistic):
- RPC/network + NLB + cross-AZ = 20–50ms (if cross-AZ present; single AZ typically 5–15ms).
- Batch queuing delay (W) = 50–180ms depending on window and load.
- Kernel + token generation = 50–120ms for 420 tokens depending on quantization and model.
- Targeting 95th < 300ms implies batching window + generation + network must be <= ~250ms; so keep batching window <= 120ms at 95th.

Recommendation based on sim:
- Start with 16 H100s spread across 2 AZs (8/8), enable batching window of 80–120ms, autoscale target thresholds at 70% CPU/GPU util or queue depth trigger (queue depth > 40 across pool) to add 1 GPU.
- Maintain 2 hot-warm GPUs per AZ to handle immediate spikes without full allocation latency. Warm nodes should have warmed KV caches and preloaded weights; using our prefetch hooks lowers first-request penalty to ~50ms.
- For procurement ask: list both on-demand burst capacity (if cloud provider supports warm standby) and reserved baseline (16 GPUs).

Notes on graceful degradation:
- Quantized model reduces kernel latency by ~30–45% on H100 for your model family; useful as mid-tier fallback before switching to smaller architecture.
- If queueing depth persists > 120s (extreme), implement per-tenant rate limits and notify product owners.

I'll leave the sim CSV with a few curves (steady, 2x spike, 4x spike) — it shows latency percentiles for each fleet size. Happy to run a live single-tenant test harness if Zephyr can provide a test endpoint.

—Marcus

Tessa/Marcus —

Thanks, this is exactly the level of detail we needed. We'll take the 16 H100 baseline + 2 warm GPUs approach into procurement and schedule a 30-min sync next week to review the sim CSV before finalizing.

Can you confirm whether the 2 warm GPUs need to be identical H100s or if N1-standard warm instances with preloaded weights + cold-start optimization suffice for the burst buffer?

Alex
